newsitem.title: UK: Euro clauses key Eurobond development in January.
newsitem.headline: Euro clauses key Eurobond development in January.

text.p: The use of language governing the euro's inception was the major innovation in the staid Eurobond market in January amid record-breaking issuance.
The language, primarily clauses allowing for redenomination into the euro, should improve liquidity after the third stage of European economic and monetary union scheduled for January 1999.
Three major benchmark Eurobonds contained the new language.
The first was a French franc issue from Austria.

The second and third were both from the European Investment Bank (EIB). These were a 10-year guilder issue and, today, a deal due April 2004 advertised by the leads as being a 1.0 billion euro Eurobond.
However, the deal will be paid for in Ecu and so will all coupons until such time as the Euro is adopted, if ever.
Managers closely involved with the deals were enthusiastic, saying the bonds would improve liquidity throughout Europe after EMU because investors' scope would be greatly widened.
Investors now confined to, say, mark issues would in future have the freedom to invest in borrowers who had previously been confined to issuing in French francs or guilders, etc.
But syndicate managers not connected to any of the three deals downplayed their significance.
"They're no different to a regular French franc or Dutch guilder deal," said a U.S. bank syndicate manager.
"You have the potential for advanced liquidity in the situation where the Euro becomes a single currency. But it doesn't effect the performance of the bond now."
Traditionally a busy month for market, January saw issuance top $85 billion, eclipsing the record-breaking $75 billion launched in January 1996.
Dollar deals dominated, accounting for 42 percent of the market, in line with its 41 percent for all of 1996.

"There was a shortfall in supply after the high level of redemptions at the end of last year," a syndicate manager at a leading U.S. bank said. "That combined with issuers' eagerness to get in quickly at the start of the year".
Elsewhere in January, two clear favourites emerged from amongst the high-yielding currencies.

The Czech crown saw over 20 bonds worth over $1.0 billion launched, with the sector attracting a host of prominent, top-rated retail-friendly names. Issuance has been very short-dated due to an inverted Czech yield curve.
Demand was driven by the crown's stability which is boosting confidence. "Investors are buying into a positive currency story" said Jan Pudil a banker at WoodCommerz in Prague.
The rand sector also took the market by storm.
Gerry Moes, syndicate chief at Hambros said much of the demand came from investors rolling over investments from maturing bonds.
Dealers said investors were reinvesting to avoid realising currency losses caused by the rand's depreciation in 1996.
Moes at Hambros said the more positive feel towards the rand of late, had also contributed to the demand late in the month.
Among emerging credits, Argentina and Mexico led the way with a series of chunky international bond offerings.
So called cross-over buying -- when non-emerging market specialists buy emerging market debt -- fuelled demand for dollar bonds and buoyed Latin American bonds generally.
